article_title: Exploring the dimensions of electronic work integrated learning (eWIL)
citation: Schuster, Lisa & Glavas, Charmaine (2017). Exploring the dimensions of electronic work integrated learning (eWIL). Educational Research Review, 21, pp. 55-66. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2017.04.001
title: Two-dimensional typology of eWIL: function of technology (support vs. deliver) by degree of technological involvement (low vs. high)
description: The review develops a typology classifying eWIL experiences along two dimensions: the function of the technology (supporting administrative WIL processes vs. delivering the WIL experience pedagogically) and the degree of technological involvement (low vs. high). Iterative open and pattern coding of 22 studies produced "four broad codes: "Technology-Supported", "Technology-Facilitated", "Technology-Blended" and "Technology-Based"", validated by independent recoding with no inconsistencies between researchers. The typology extends Kaider et al. (2009) by recognizing that technology can deliver, not just support, WIL.
requirements: Studies must be classifiable by both the function the technology serves in the WIL experience and the extent of technological involvement
constraints: The authors acknowledge that theoretically there are likely to be numerous attributes which may influence the implementation of the typology, and the study aimed to identify preliminary attributes rather than be exhaustive
target_learners: higher education students participating in work integrated learning
examples: Technology-Supported: a web-based portal for industry partners; Technology-Facilitated: digital platforms such as OpenSim used to prepare students; Technology-Blended: face-to-face placements combined with online role-plays; Technology-Based: WIL through virtual reality
key_sources: Schuster, Lisa & Glavas, Charmaine (2017). Exploring the dimensions of electronic work integrated learning (eWIL). Educational Research Review, 21, pp. 55-66. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2017.04.001

article_title: Getting Students on Track for Graduation: Impacts of the Early Warning Intervention and Monitoring System after One Year. REL 2017-272
citation: Faria, A.-M., Sorensen, N., Heppen, J., Bowdon, J., Taylor, S., Eisner, R., & Foster, S. (2017). Getting students on track for graduation: Impacts of the Early Warning Intervention and Monitoring System after one year (REL 2017–272). Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Regional Educational Laboratory Midwest. http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/edlabs
title: Early Warning Intervention and Monitoring System (EWIMS) seven-step process and early warning data tool
description: EWIMS is a systematic approach to identifying students at risk of not graduating on time, assigning them to interventions, and monitoring their progress. Schools implement a seven-step process—establishing a team, using the early warning data tool, reviewing and interpreting data, assigning and providing interventions, monitoring students, and evaluating and refining the process—supported by an early warning data tool that "automatically flags students as at risk using thresholds based on prior research". The tool's indicators include chronic absence, course failure, low GPA, behavior, and an off-track flag. EWIMS does not prescribe specific interventions; schools inventory available interventions and match them to flagged students' needs.
requirements: A school-based EWIMS team with broad staff representation that meets monthly and examines risk status at the end of each grading period
Import of student demographic, attendance, course failure, GPA, and behavior data into the early warning data tool
A locally available catalog of interventions to which flagged students can be assigned
constraints: EWIMS does not prescribe specific interventions; effectiveness depends on the quality and appropriateness of the support provided
Implementation was challenging in the first year of adoption, with overall implementation low across participating schools
target_learners: First- and second-year high school students at risk of not graduating on time
target_learning_goals: Staying on track for on-time high school graduation through improved attendance, course performance, behavior, and credit accumulation
examples: In the study, 37 high schools implemented EWIMS during 2014/15 with technical assistance liaisons delivering 11 trainings between April 2014 and June 2015
key_sources: Faria, A.-M., Sorensen, N., Heppen, J., Bowdon, J., Taylor, S., Eisner, R., & Foster, S. (2017). Getting students on track for graduation: Impacts of the Early Warning Intervention and Monitoring System after one year (REL 2017–272). Washington, DC: U.S. Department of Education, Institute of Education Sciences, National Center for Education Evaluation and Regional Assistance, Regional Educational Laboratory Midwest. http://ies.ed.gov/ncee/edlabs

article_title: Effects of Reflective Inquiry Instructional Technique on Students' Academic Achievement and Ability Level in Electronic Work Trade in Technical Colleges
citation: Dr (Mrs) T. C. Ogbuanya & Dr A. S. Owodunni. (2015). Effects of Reflective Inquiry Instructional Technique on Students' Academic Achievement and Ability Level in Electronic Work Trade in Technical Colleges. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.7. https://www.iiste.org
title: Electronic Works Achievement Test (EWAT)
description: The EWAT is the researcher-developed achievement instrument used to measure learning outcomes in the study. It "consists of 30 - multiple choice items with five options" built from the CRT 12 (Electronic Devices and Circuits) module and the NBTE 2008 curriculum blueprint. Its reliability coefficient was 0.83 via test-retest with Pearson Product Moment Correlation, and all 30 items showed good difficulty, discrimination and distractor indices.
requirements: Face and content validation by Electronic Works lecturers and measurement and evaluation experts
Items meeting Difficulty Index 20-80, discrimination of 0.20 and above, and negative distractor indices
target_learners: Technical college Electronic Works trade students
target_learning_goals: Electronic Works trade achievement (Electronic Devices and Circuits module)
examples: Administered as pretest on day one and as posttest after the ten-week treatment to both experimental and control groups
key_sources: Dr (Mrs) T. C. Ogbuanya & Dr A. S. Owodunni. (2015). Effects of Reflective Inquiry Instructional Technique on Students' Academic Achievement and Ability Level in Electronic Work Trade in Technical Colleges. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.6, No.7. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1083083

article_title: The moderating effect of team-based learning participation frequency on the relationship between medical students' perception of systematic team-based learning class management and active class participation.
citation: Jeong Somi, Kim Seung Jung, Lee Kyoung Eun, Ko Ara. (2025). The moderating effect of team-based learning participation frequency on the relationship between medical students’ perception of systematic team-based learning class management and active class participation. Korean Journal of Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.3946/kjme.2025.346
title: Ewha TBL end-of-session feedback questionnaire measuring perceived systematic management, active participation, and satisfaction
description: A three-variable feedback questionnaire administered at the end of each TBL session at Ewha Womans University College of Medicine, developed by the College's TBL Board of four clinical professors "with an average of over 15 years of educational experience" and validated by content experts. It measures perception of systematic TBL class management (4 items, Cronbach's α=0.871), active class participation (2 items, α=0.861), and class satisfaction, all on a 4-point agreement scale. The study used it to measure its primary variables.
requirements: Administered at the end of each TBL session
constraints: The article states the measurement tools were developed primarily for feedback purposes rather than being validated research instruments
key_sources: Jeong Somi, Kim Seung Jung, Lee Kyoung Eun, Ko Ara. (2025). The moderating effect of team-based learning participation frequency on the relationship between medical students’ perception of systematic team-based learning class management and active class participation. Korean Journal of Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.3946/kjme.2025.346
